pendingReview.title: Smartphone learns to find hidden cameras in five seconds | NEWS.am TECH - Innovations and science
pendingReview.description: Engineers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have developed SweepLED, a system that turns an ordinary smartphone into a hidden-camera detector. The device uses a specialised case equipped with LEDs and machine learning algorithms to identify spy lenses in rental apartments and hotels. Why Conventional Methods Fall Short Traditional ways of locating hidden cameras often prove unreliable. The usual approach involves scanning a room and looking for bright reflections from lenses. The problem is that glossy buttons, metallic furniture fittings, and other shiny surfaces reflect light almost as effectively as camera lenses. As a result, sensors regularly produce false positives, leaving users without full confidence in the room's safety. How SweepLED Works The new system addresses this problem with a case fitted with an array of LEDs. The user points the smartphone camera at a suspicious object and holds the device steady at three different angles. Meanwhile, the LEDs scan the surface with varying illumination, and the phone's camera captures the subtlest changes in reflected light. A neural network analyses the series of images and identifies spatiotemporal reflection patterns. Hidden camera lenses have complex internal structures, so they respond to changes in lighting angle differently from ordinary shiny objects. It is precisely this distinction that allows the system to tell a genuine lens from an everyday reflection. How Effective Is It In tests on 30 objects, the system achieved 94% accuracy during manual scanning. The entire process takes less than five seconds. The developers emphasise that this approach significantly reduces false alarms compared with conventional detectors. Why This Matters The issue of hidden cameras in rental accommodation has reached global proportions. Travellers regularly face the risk of illegal recording, and short-term rental platforms cannot always guarantee safety. Cameras are concealed in clocks, power sockets, smoke detectors, and other household items. SweepLED allows guests to check a room using a familiar smartphone and an additional case. This makes inspection simpler and more accessible for ordinary travellers. In Brief Engineers at KAIST have created SweepLED -- a case with LEDs and a machine learning algorithm that turns a smartphone into a hidden-camera detector. The device scans a surface from different angles and, based on reflection patterns, distinguishes camera lenses from ordinary shiny objects. In tests, accuracy reached 94%, and a scan takes less than five seconds. The development is intended to help travellers find spy cameras in rented accommodation more quickly.

pendingReview.title: Researchers come up with a hidden camera detector for just $7
pendingReview.description: Its LED case components cost less than $7, but the tool is not commercially available yet. Researchers are addressing the stalking problem by creating technology that helps detect secret cameras with a phone. There have been multiple horror stories where people have been filmed without their consent, including hidden cameras in Airbnbs, changing rooms, and even toilets. Online tutorials proliferated showing users where to check and how to spot such cameras. However, these searches usually involve a human eye and its perceptual judgment. Now, researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have developed an AI tool that turns a smartphone into a device for detecting hidden cameras. KAIST's research team created "SweepLED" technology, which consists of a device with 15 LEDs attached to a phone and an AI-powered processing system. The technology works by attaching an LED light to a smartphone's camera, illuminating objects while the camera is on. Then it analyzes the patterns of light reflections that were cast. While reflections on regular objects move or disappear, hidden camera lenses appear in those reflection patterns. The SweepLED system has already been used to test 30 objects and achieved approximately 94% detection accuracy, according to KAIST. The device took around 5 seconds to scan an object. What makes this technology even more beneficial is that the components in the LED case cost less than $7, making it an affordable solution that more people can use. The LED light-powered technology isn't yet commercially available, but it does show potential. "This research is meaningful in that it combines low-cost smartphone-based hardware with AI analysis to present the possibility of a practical detection technology that even non-experts can use," Professor Jun Han, who led the research, told Eureka Alert.

pendingReview.title: Francisco Munoz Charged With Secretly Recording Children As They Changed Clothes
pendingReview.description: SANTA PAULA, Calif. (KEYT) - Francisco Munoz of Santa Paula has been charged after allegedly recording children changing in an office bathroom at the apartment complex where he worked. Investigators believe that their may be additional survivors that have yet to be identified from the secretly recorded videos. Anyone with more information is asked to contact Detective Yvette Solis at 805-826-7512 or through email at ysolis@santapaula.gov. On Aug. 24, around 4:45 p.m., officers responded to the 200 block of North 8th Street for a report about a man covertly filming children changing clothes in an apartment complex office bathroom after using a nearby pool stated the Santa Paula Police Department. Detectives quickly identified the suspect as 48-year-old Francisco Munoz, an employee of the apartment complex, who fled the scene before the arrival of police shared the Santa Paula Police Department. A search was conducted and eventually, the Santa Paula man was arrested later the same afternoon noted the law enforcement ageny. According to Santa Paula Police, Munoz is alleged to have used a makeshift box with a hole, hid a cell phone inside of the box, and video recorded multiple minors as they changed in the bathroom. On Aug. 26, Munoz was arraigned in Ventura County Superior Court on the following charges: * PC 647(j)(3)-Using a Hidden Camera to Secretly Record Someone Who Is Partially or Fully Undressed in a Private Location * Multiple Counts of PC 647.6(a)(1)-Child Annoying * Multiple Counts of PC 311.4(c)-Using a Minor for Child Pornography * PC 311.11(a)(1)-Possession of Child Pornography Munoz remains in custody added the Santa Paula Police Department.
